newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain to approve austere budget despite critics.
newsitem.headline: Spain to approve austere budget despite critics.

text.p: Spain's conservative government officially presents its first budget to parliament on Monday, an austere set of measures which is certain to be approved despite sharp criticism from the leftist opposition.

The package, unveiled on Friday, slashes spending with unpopular measures which the minority Popular Party (PP) government hopes will shape up the nation for the launch of a single European currency in 1999.

Spending has been cut or frozen in all sectors except for pensions, health and regional transfers and is due to grow by a mere 1.7 percent in 1997, making this the most restrictive budget since Spain's return to democracy in 1975.
The PP has already secured the support of its Catalan nationalist allies in parliament, ensuring the budget will be voted through next month.
But unions and left-wing parties attacked the plan this weekend, saying that despite its lofty goals it lacks credibility and places the burden of budget adjustment on the poorest sectors of society.
"This is the most restrictive budget in many years," Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar conceded in an interview with Catalan daily La Vanguardia.
But he added that it was based on social dialogue, which had produced an agreement on pensions with unions last week.
The PP says the budget will not only allow Spain to be among the first members of European economic and monetary union (EMU) but also fuel growth and create badly-needed jobs for Spaniards.

"The budget we are going to implement is the one Spaniards want," Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato told daily El Pais. "We are not looking at a depressive budget; I think it guarantees recovery," he said in the interview published on Sunday.

The Socialists, in opposition after 13 years at the helm, back the PP's commitment to EMU but criticise the means. They accuse the conservatives of short-termism, saying their figures are over-optimistic and don't add up.

"It's bread for today and hunger for tomorrow," said Jose Borrell, budget spokesman for the Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE). "In reality, this group of creative accounting measures do nothing but delay the deficit to future years."

In particular, a freeze on public wages next year threatens the recovery of consumer demand and makes the government's target of three percent economic growth all but impossible, according to the PSOE.
Opposition groups also accuse the PP of selling out to the Catalans by pandering to the nationalists' demands on health spending and regional transfers, at the expense of less powerful interests.

Although the Socialists have no power to block the budget from being made law, a spokesman said they may send it back for amendment once they have read the full text of the draft, due to be handed to parliament on Monday.
Meanwhile, unions say they will protest the wage freeze despite last week's pension deal and go ahead with planned demonstrations on Monday and October 15.

"They started with giving fiscal gifts to the richest and now they want to compensate for it by sacrificing the salaries of public workers, by imposing taxes, by raising indirect taxes, which families with medium or low wages will pay," said Antonio Gutierrez, secretary general of Workers' Commissions (CCOO).
Jordi Pujol, leader of the Catalan Convergence and Unity (CiU) coalition, has declared himself pleased with the budget although provisions for health spending only half satisfied his party's goals.
"With this budget, the Bank of Spain will understand that the government's policy is serious and truly orthodox and that there will therefore be a cut in interest rates," he said on Saturday.

Economists expect the Bank of Spain to express its approval by cutting its key money market rate -- the rate at which it lends to other banks -- by up to half-a-point from 7.25 percent at its next regular auction on Thursday. REUTER
